The Final Second Reviewer found that Mr. Wu was not eligible for the Canada Recovery Benefit [CRB] because he did not earn at least $5,000 (before taxes) of CRB eligible employment or net self-employment income in 2019, 2020, or in the 12 months before the date of his first application.

[3] In response, the Respondent, the Attorney General of Canada [AGC], raises as a preliminary issue, the admissibility of some of the evidence contained in Mr. Wu’s Application Record. V. Standard of Review [31] The presumptive standard of review is reasonableness: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 10, 25. To avoid intervention on judicial review, the decision must bear the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility: Vavilov at para 99. A reasonable decision will always depend on the constraints imposed by the legal and factual context of the particular decision under review: Vavilov at para 90. The Court must avoid reassessing and reweighing the evidence before the decision-maker; a decision may be unreasonable, however, if the decision-maker “fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it”: Vavilov at paras 125-126.

[32] The party challenging the decision bears the onus of demonstrating that the decision is unreasonable: Vavilov at para 100. For the reviewing Court to intervene, the party challenging the decision must satisfy the Court that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” and that the alleged flaws “must be more than merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision”: Vavilov at para 100. The reviewing Court must ultimately be satisfied that the decision-maker’s reasoning “adds up”: Vavilov at para 104.

[53] Mr. Wu submits that the CRA breached its duty of procedural fairness by failing to consider the documentation he submitted showing that he earned the required income of $5,000. Mr. Wu refers broadly and generally to electronic money transfers, employer’s letter of confirmation of employment, T4 slips, tax returns, receipts and invoices. Mr. Wu argues that, by proceeding “directly to recovery”, the CRA denied him a “fair opportunity to respond.”

[54] To support his procedural fairness argument, Mr. Wu refers to Cameron v Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FC 2 [Cameron]. In Cameron, the Court found that there was a breach of procedural fairness because the CRA failed to act on its representations and failed to accommodate the applicant’s disability. The CRA was aware of the applicant’s disability requiring communications in writing and that by failing to provide same, the applicant did not have an opportunity to know his case and respond to it: Cameron at para 34, citing Canadian Pacific at para 56. The Court added that this finding is buttressed by a breach of the doctrine of legitimate expectations whereby a CRA supervisor made clear, unambiguous and unqualified representations to the applicant that a particular procedure would be followed, and ultimately it was not: Cameron at para 35, citing Agraira v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 at para 96.

Furthermore, his broad argument that he was not provided with a “fair opportunity to respond” to the CRA is not borne out by the facts of this matter. Quite the contrary. As shown above, Mr. Wu was provided with six phone calls explaining the types of documents he needed to submit, and in fact submitted additional documents to the CRA on five different occasions, namely on August 4, 2022, December 15, 2022, February 7, 2024, May 24, 2024, and June 28, 2024.

[56] I find that there was no breach of procedural fairness in this matter. Mr. Wu had a full and fair opportunity to know the case, that he had to meet and was provided with a meaningful opportunity to respond.

[57] Mr. Wu also argues that procedural fairness was breached because he was coerced “into agreeing with a fabricated reason” and that coercion by a government official is an abuse of administrative discretion, resulting in an infringement of his section 7 Charter rights to liberty and security of the person against arbitrary state laws, which in turn, justifies the granting of extraordinary remedies including mandamus. In his written materials, Mr. Wu does not identify a specific instance of coercion, nor does he rely on any relevant authorities to make this argument. At the hearing, it became apparent that Mr. Wu was referring to his allegation being coerced by the CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455 into saying that the sums he received from Mr. Lau were a gift.

[58] There is no evidence before this Court of any coercion on the part of the CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455 who obtained the information from Mr. Wu on his non-profit services to Mr. Lau. REASONS AND JUDGMENT

I. Overview [1] The Applicant, Mr. Jimmy N.H. Wu, is a self-represented litigant who seeks judicial review of a decision made by a benefits validation officer [Final Second Reviewer] of the Canada Revenue Agency [CRA], dated August 1, 2024, [Final Second Review Decision]. The Final Second Reviewer found that Mr. Wu was not eligible for the Canada Recovery Benefit [CRB] because he did not earn at least $5,000 (before taxes) of CRB eligible employment or net self-employment income in 2019, 2020, or in the 12 months before the date of his first application.

[2] Mr. Wu submits that the Final Second Reviewer breached his right to procedural fairness by failing to consider the documentation he submitted. Mr. Wu submits that the Final Second Review Decision is unreasonable because “CRA’s conclusion that [he] did not meet the $5,000 income threshold lacks justification, as it ignores documentary proof of income”. Mr. Wu also alleges that he was coerced into “agreeing with a fabricated reason” that money he had received from helping an elderly gentleman was a “gift”, which he argues resulted in a breach of his rights guaranteed by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s 7, Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982, being Schedule B to the Canada Act 1982 (UK), 1982, c 11 [Charter].

[3] In response, the Respondent, the Attorney General of Canada [AGC], raises as a preliminary issue, the admissibility of some of the evidence contained in Mr. Wu’s Application Record. Moreover, the AGC submits the Final Second Review Decision is reasonable and was rendered in a procedurally fair manner.

[4] Though I am mindful of the fact that Mr. Wu is a self-represented litigant, for the following reasons, and in conformity with the role of this Court in a judicial review, I find that the Final Second Review Decision was arrived at in a procedurally fair manner and is not unreasonable. It would be improper for this Court, in the legal framework of judicial review, to give Mr. Wu yet another chance to provide additional evidence to the CRA when he failed to do so, despite the multiple opportunities afforded to him by the CRA.

II. Background A. Relevant Legislation [5] For the purposes of this application for judicial review, the relevant CRB eligibility requirements found at subsection 3(1) of the Canada Recovery Benefits Act, SC 2020, c 12, s 2 [CRB Act], are applicable:

[6] Other relevant provisions of the CRB Act are section 2, which defines the proper Minister; section 6, which confers the burden of proof to the taxpayer; and subsection 30(1), which permits the Minister of Employment and Social Development to reconsider eligibility for the CRB after the benefit has been paid:
Definitions
2 The following definitions apply in this Act.
[…]
Minister means the Minister of Employment and Social Development. (ministre)
Définitions
2 Les définitions qui suivent s’appliquent à la présente loi.
[…]
ministre Le ministre de l’Emploi et du Développement social. (Minister)
Obligation to provide information
6 An applicant must provide the Minister with any information that the Minister may require in respect of the application.
Reconsideration of application
30 (1) Subject to subsection (5), the Minister may re-consider an application for benefits under this Act within 36 months after the benefits have been paid.
Obligation de fournir des renseignements
6 Le demandeur fournit au ministre tout renseignement que ce dernier peut exiger relativement à la demande.
Nouvelle examen de la demande
30 (1) Sous réserve du paragraphe (5), le ministre peut examiner de nouveau toute demande de prestation au titre de la présente loi dans les trente-six mois qui suivent le versement des prestations.
B. Facts (1) Application for CRB [7] On October 28, 2020, Mr. Wu first applied for and eventually received the CRB for the periods from October 11 to October 24, 2020, and subsequently received the CRB for the periods from January 3 to October 23, 2021.
(2) First Decision [8] On June 30, 2022, (and then again on August 16, 2022), the CRA sent a letter to Mr. Wu advising that it would conduct a verification review of his eligibility for the CRB. The letter outlined the income requirement, listed acceptable forms of proof of earnings over $5,000, and requested that Mr. Wu provide his supporting documentation.

[10] In the notes dated November 15, 2022, the Officer with user ID number VWL243 [First Reviewer] determined that Mr. Wu was not eligible for the CRB as the documents submitted were not sufficient to confirm that he met the income requirement of $5,000 and that Mr. Wu could not be reached for further information [First Decision].

[13] In the notes dated August 9, 2023, the Officer with user ID number HCD573 [Initial Second Reviewer] found that Mr. Wu was not eligible for the CRB as the documents submitted were not sufficient to confirm that Mr. Wu met the income requirement of $5,000 [Initial Second Decision], and that Mr. Wu could not be contacted for further information after two attempts.

[14] By letter dated August 15, 2023, the CRA notified Mr. Wu of the Initial Second Review Decision of the Initial Second Reviewer, indicating that based on the CRA’s review, Mr. Wu is not eligible for the CRB because he did not earn at least $5,000 (before taxes) of employment or net self-employment income in 2019, 2020, or in the 12 months before the date of his first application.
(4) Second Review Process Leading up to Final Second Review Decision [15] Following the Initial Second Review Decision, the CRA assigned a different Officer with user ID number WCZ817 to conduct another review of Mr. Wu’s CRB eligibility.

[16] On January 16, 2024, the Officer with user ID number WCZ817 spoke with Mr. Wu over the phone. The notes from the conversation indicate that Mr. Wu was interested in having his CRB eligibility reviewed again. Mr. Wu explained he was receiving employment insurance benefits in the beginning of 2019 until sometime in March of 2019. He added that he started babysitting in June of 2019 until December 2019. Mr. Wu confirmed that the child he was babysitting was his nephew, that he was paid in cash each time and did not deposit the money in his bank account. Mr. Wu stated he never babysat other children and never intended to continue doing so; he was doing it to help his brother. Mr. Wu then explained his 2020 income was earned from his employment as a cleaner with AromaOasis, where he was also paid in cash and never deposited in his bank account. He was laid off in March 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Officer notes having “went over all possible documentation he could have”, but Mr. Wu noted he only had verbal agreements with her employers.

[18] On March 13, 2024, the Officer with user ID number WCZ817 called Mr. Wu to ask follow-up questions. Mr. Wu explained that he was diagnosed with cancer at the end of 2018 and was receiving employment insurance sickness benefits until March of 2019. He was then unable to return to his past employment as a security guard, so he started babysitting his nephew for his brother who had just moved from China. He stopped babysitting in December 2019 because his brother went on a holiday. Upon their return, he did not start babysitting again because he was too busy with his cleaning job at AromaOasis, where he cleaned a clinic. He mentioned the clinic shut down in March 2020 because of the pandemic. Mr. Wu further stated that he did not work the rest of the 2020 year because of cancer treatments but did also say he sent out some resumes but had no success. Mr. Wu did not have any documentation of this at the time to support these statements. Mr. Wu confirmed he did not work in 2021 and only found employment again in June 2022.

[19] On May 15, 2024, the Officer with user ID number WCZ817 called Mr. Wu again to follow up. The Officer with user ID number WCZ817 explained that the income from babysitting his nephew would be considered casual income, and not business income, because his nephew was his only client and he previously stated he was only doing it to help his brother and had no intentions of making this a business. Mr. Wu then stated he forgot to mention that he was helping a senior named A. Lau, and feels like this makes him a self-employed caregiver. This work would have been performed in 2019, and he would have been paid by cheques. Mr. Wu could not confirm if the AromaOasis clinic closed because of the pandemic, but he would try to confirm. Mr. Wu requested until May 31, 2024, to submit other documents.
[21] In June 2024, another CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455, was assigned to review Mr. Wu’s CRB eligibility.

[22] On June 14, 2024, the Officer with user ID number XHJ455 called Mr. Wu, who once again explained he was employed at a health clinic as a cleaner until March 2020. Mr. Wu claimed he applied to many jobs during the pandemic but got no response, which is why he applied for the CRB. Mr. Wu explained that in 2019, he babysat his nephew and made a total of $3,700 in cash and never deposited it into his account. Mr. Wu then explained that he was helping a senior with daily tasks, such as grocery shopping and cleaning his house, but that he was not paid regularly, although the senior gentleman gave him cheques as pay sometimes. When asked if these cheques could be considered as gifts, Mr. Wu said “yes”. Mr. Wu then stated that he earned $2,000 from his work as a cleaner for the health clinic. The Officer with user ID number XHJ455 then explained to Mr. Wu that the documents on file were not sufficient to prove his eligibility and gave Mr. Wu until June 27, 2024, to provide more documentation, including “receipts from Dr. Gao; T4 slip from clinic, employment letter including details of record of employment, communication record (text message, emails) to verify the employment.”
[24] In July 2024, another CRA officer with user ID CLX248 [Final Second Reviewer] was assigned to continue the second review of Mr. Wu’s CRB eligibility.
[25] On July 17, 2024, the Final Second Reviewer spoke to Mr. Wu on the phone, and confirmed the information already mentioned above.

[26] On July 29, 2024, the Final Second Reviewer spoke to Mr. Wu on the phone to explain to him how the review would be conducted, notably that because each benefit had a different application date, different periods would be used to calculate the required income of $5,000.
III. Decision Under Review [27] By letter addressed to Mr. Wu and dated August 1, 2024, the Final Second Reviewer concluded that Mr. Wu was not eligible for the CRB because he did not earn $5,000 (before taxes) of employment and/or self-employment income in 2019, 2020, or in the 12 months before the date of his application [Final Second Review Decision].

[28] The Final Second Reviewer’s notes dated July 29, 2024, form part of the reasons for the Final Second Review Decision: Aryan v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FC 139 [Aryan] at para 22. In the notes, the Final Second Reviewer lists the new documents filed by Mr. Wu on May 24, 2024, and June 28, 2024, as well as a summary from their conversation with Mr. Wu on July 17, 2024. The Final Second Reviewer notes that there are no calculations to be done and that Mr. Wu’s income on file is as follows:
2019 – Net Self Employment Income $3750;
2020 – Net Self Employment Income $2000; and
2021 – No eligible Income on file.

[29] The Final Second Reviewer’s analysis is documented in a note dated July 29, 2024, part of which is reproduced below:
Decision: CRB ineligible for periods 2, 8-28 for not meeting 5k income criteria in 2019, 2020 or in the 12 months prior to the application of employment and/or net self-employment income (2019-10-28 to 2020-10-28).
The benefit recipient (BR) provided 15 receipts from June 2019 to December 2019 showing bi-weekly payments of $250.00 total $3750, 3 invoices from Jennifer Gao totaling $2000 from January 2020 to March 2020, screenshots of job applications for 2020 and 2021, letter from Employer Jennifer Gao from Aromaoasis, A copy of Wai Man Chen Tax return showing $3750 claimed for child care, A copy of a T4A from Aromaoasis, Lifelabs reports, 3 copies of cheques from Alan Lau to Jimmy Wu in 2019 and 2020.
The receipts the BR provided from babysitting and cleaning from November 2019 to March of 2020 total $3250.
The BR did not earn $5000 in 2019 or 2020 and the amount that was earned in the 12 months prior to his application 2019-10-28 to 2020-10-28 do not equal the required $5000 income threshold in employment income or self employment income to be eligible for the CRB.
[…]
IV. Issues [30] There are four issues before me that I reproduce below, with the first two being preliminary issues raised by the AGC, followed by the two issues raised by Mr. Wu:
Whether Mr. Wu has properly named the Respondent?
Whether Mr. Wu’s newly submitted evidence should be considered by the Court?
Whether the Final Second Review Decision is unreasonable?
Whether the Final Second Review Decision was arrived at in a procedurally unfair manner?

V. Standard of Review [31] The presumptive standard of review is reasonableness: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 10, 25. To avoid intervention on judicial review, the decision must bear the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility: Vavilov at para 99. A reasonable decision will always depend on the constraints imposed by the legal and factual context of the particular decision under review: Vavilov at para 90. The Court must avoid reassessing and reweighing the evidence before the decision-maker; a decision may be unreasonable, however, if the decision-maker “fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it”: Vavilov at paras 125-126.

[32] The party challenging the decision bears the onus of demonstrating that the decision is unreasonable: Vavilov at para 100. For the reviewing Court to intervene, the party challenging the decision must satisfy the Court that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” and that the alleged flaws “must be more than merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision”: Vavilov at para 100. The reviewing Court must ultimately be satisfied that the decision-maker’s reasoning “adds up”: Vavilov at para 104.

[33] Breaches of procedural fairness in administrative contexts have been considered reviewable on a correctness standard or subject to a “reviewing exercise is ‘best reflected in the correctness standard’ even though, strictly speaking, no standard of review is being applied”: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 [Canadian Pacific] at para 54. The duty of procedural fairness “is ‘eminently variable’, inherently flexible and context-specific”; it must be determined with reference to all the circumstances, including the non-exhaustive list of factors referenced in Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paragraphs 22-23: Vavilov at para 77. In sum, the focus of the reviewing court is whether the process was fair. In the words of the Federal Court of Appeal, the ultimate or fundamental questions are:

[56] No matter how much deference is accorded administrative tribunals in the exercise of their discretion to make procedural choices, the ultimate question remains whether the applicant knew the case to meet and had a full and fair chance to respond. It would be problematic if an a priori decision as to whether the standard of review is correctness or reasonableness generated a different answer to what is a singular question that is fundamental to the concept of justice―was the party given a right to be heard and the opportunity to know the case against them? Procedural fairness is not sacrificed on the altar of deference.
Canadian Pacific at para 56 [emphasis added].

VI. Analysis A. Whether Mr. Wu has properly named the Respondent? [34] As a preliminary matter, the Respondent’s Memorandum of Fact and Law indicates that the “Attorney General of Canada”, and not the CRA, should be named as the Respondent in this matter. I agree with the AGC that the CRA is not the proper Respondent as it is not directly affected by the order sought in this application for judicial review: Rule 303 of the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106; Aryan at para 13. The proper responding party is the “Attorney General of Canada”, because Mr. Wu is challenging the Final Second Review Decision made by the Final Second Reviewer of the CRA on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Social Development: definition of “Minister” at section 2 of the CRB Act reproduced above.
[37] I agree with the AGC.

[38] In the normal course, evidence that was not before the decision-maker and that goes to the merits of the matter is not admissible in an application for judicial review before this Court: Access Copyright at para 19. In Access Copyright, the Federal Court of Appeal held, at paragraph 20, that there are a few recognized exceptions to the general rule, which “exist only in situations where the receipt of the evidence by the Court is not inconsistent with the differing roles of the judicial review court and the administrative decision-maker”. The Federal Court of Appeal listed three non-exhaustive exceptions, which I summarized below:
Where the new evidence provides general background information in circumstances where that information might assist in understanding the issues relevant to the judicial review but does not add new evidence on the merits;
Where the new evidence brings to the attention of the reviewing court procedural defects not found in the evidentiary record of the decision-maker; and
Where the new evidence highlights the complete absence of evidence before the decision-maker on a particular finding.
Access Copyright at para 20.

[39] I am not satisfied that the above-referenced parts of the exhibits “D”, “L”, “M”, “N” and “O” included in Mr. Wu’s affidavit meet any of the Access Copyright exceptions. They do not provide general background information and do not aim to demonstrate a breach in procedural fairness or the complete absence of evidence before the decision-maker. Rather, most of them aim at supplementing Mr. Wu’s evidence that he wishes he had submitted to the Final Second Reviewer. Admitting any of the documents into evidence would be inconsistent with this Court’s role to review the Final Second Review Decision based upon the facts and record that were before them: Federal Courts Act, RSC 1985, c F-7, s 18.1(4)(d); Access Copyright at para 20.

[40] Therefore, the new evidence is not admissible and will not be considered. On judicial review, the role of this Court is not to consider the matter on the merits again, but to review the Final Second Review Decision to ensure it is reasonable and was made in a procedurally fair manner.
C. Whether the Final Second Review Decision is unreasonable? [41] The burden is on Mr. Wu, as the challenging party, to demonstrate that the Final Second Review Decision is unreasonable. The Court must be satisfied “that there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, transparency and intelligibility”: Vavilov at para 100.

[42] Mr. Wu has not raised any serious shortcomings in the Final Second Review Decision. Flaws must be more than superficial for the reviewing court to overturn an administrative decision: Vavilov at para 100.

[43] First, Mr. Wu submits that, since he was found eligible for the CERB, this eligibility should be applied in the same way for the CRB. As the AGC submits, this Court has confirmed that the CRB is separate and distinct from the CERB, each with their own eligibility requirements: Joodaki v Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FC 260 at para 17. I cannot therefore give way to Mr. Wu’s argument. The Final Second Reviewer had to assess the eligibility for each benefit separately, which is what happened in this case.

[44] Second, Mr. Wu submits that he applied for the CRB on October 9, 2020, which means that all earnings from October 15, 2019, to October 9, 2020, can be added up to $5,000 to become eligible for CRB. Mr. Wu argues that this would include the following income amounts:
October 18 – December 27, 2019: $1,500 from babysitting for his brother (Respondent’s Record [RR] at 54-55);
December 2019 – March 2020: $2,200 from Richmond Community Benefit Program Centre (AR at 50); and
January 31 – March 12, 2020: $2,000 from AromaOasis (RR at 51).

[45] Mr. Wu argues that the Final Second Review Decision lacks justification under the Vavilov framework because the Final Second Reviewer did not refer to his tax returns and supporting records which, according to Mr. Wu, establish that the income requirement was satisfied. While Mr. Wu does not point to specific evidence, I have looked in the parties’ respective records to try to identify potential income that the Final Second Reviewer did not consider and that could put Mr. Wu over the threshold. This evidence is examined below.

[46] In a letter from A. Lau dated May 22, 2024 included in the AR, it is indicated that Mr. Wu was paid $2,200 with cheques and cash for providing personal assistant services under the Richmond Community Benefit Program. However, as previously mentioned, this letter and evidence was not before the Final Second Reviewer who made the Final Second Review Decision. This income could not have been considered by the Final Second Reviewer since it was never submitted. One cannot fault the decision-maker for not considering evidence that was not in the record before them. I note that this is odd, given that Mr. Wu submitted a letter to the CRA on May 24, 2024, two days after the aforementioned letter from A. Lau is dated. In his letter, Mr. Wu explained the work he completed for Mr. Lau, such as taking him to doctor’s appointments, shopping, haircuts, treatments, banking, meeting, etc. Mr. Wu also explained he cooked meals, cleaned and organized Mr. Lau’s home. Mr. Wu stated he was paid a stipend from a nonprofit organization for senior citizens, called Richmond Community Benefit Program Centre. One would have expected the May 22, 2024, letter to be submitted along with the other documents submitted on May 24, 2024. However, in making the Final Second Review Decision, the Final Second Reviewer made no reference to the income Mr. Wu would have generated from his work with Mr. Lau.

[47] As part of the documents submitted by Mr. Wu on May 24, 2024, various cheques were filed:
$660 from A. Lau to Mr. Wu dated January 31, 2020 (RR at 175);
$80 from A. Lau to F.V. Wu dated January 10, 2020 (RR at 176); and
$262 dated sometime prior to October 2019 is also included, which would not count in the calculation for the October 2019 – October 2020 calculation of required income [RR at 175].

[49] Regarding the money received from Mr. Lau, the AGC admits that the Final Second Reviewer did not specifically refer to this stream of alleged income in the Final Second Review Decision. However, the AGC submits that Mr. Wu previously admitted on a phone call held on June 14, 2024, with the CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455, that these amounts could be considered as a “gift” and that he was providing non-profit services to Mr. Lau, which is why it was reasonable for the Final Second Reviewer to omit mention of these amounts. I reproduce below the relevant extracts from the June 14, 2024, call log entered by the CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455, which is evidence of the phone conversations to which I note that Mr. Wu was the one who indicated providing a non-profit service to Mr. Lau as follows:
BR stated they did a non-profit service to a senior gentleman- Alan Lau; went shopping and cleaned the house. Questioned how much they got paid per hours. BR claimed they did not ask for pay, it is more like help the senior gentleman and the senior gentleman sometimes gave them cheques as pay. I then questioned if those paid can considered as gift. BR said yes.

[50] I find that it was reasonable for the Final Second Reviewer not to consider those amounts received from Mr. Lau in the calculation because they are not eligible self-employment income. The service provided to Mr. Lau by Mr. Wu was a non-profit service, and the payments received were “gifts”. It was not a for-profit service with the intent to operate a business (to run an enterprise, to make profits or have a reasonable expectation of profit): Procedure document that instructs CRA agents on how to determine COVID-19 benefits eligibility (RR at 224).

[53] Mr. Wu submits that the CRA breached its duty of procedural fairness by failing to consider the documentation he submitted showing that he earned the required income of $5,000. Mr. Wu refers broadly and generally to electronic money transfers, employer’s letter of confirmation of employment, T4 slips, tax returns, receipts and invoices. Mr. Wu argues that, by proceeding “directly to recovery”, the CRA denied him a “fair opportunity to respond.”

[54] To support his procedural fairness argument, Mr. Wu refers to Cameron v Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FC 2 [Cameron]. In Cameron, the Court found that there was a breach of procedural fairness because the CRA failed to act on its representations and failed to accommodate the applicant’s disability. The CRA was aware of the applicant’s disability requiring communications in writing and that by failing to provide same, the applicant did not have an opportunity to know his case and respond to it: Cameron at para 34, citing Canadian Pacific at para 56. The Court added that this finding is buttressed by a breach of the doctrine of legitimate expectations whereby a CRA supervisor made clear, unambiguous and unqualified representations to the applicant that a particular procedure would be followed, and ultimately it was not: Cameron at para 35, citing Agraira v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 at para 96.

[55] The Cameron decision does not assist Mr. Wu in making his procedural unfairness argument, as the underlying facts are different as he is not disabled and was not promised that a particular procedure would be followed that ultimately was not. Furthermore, his broad argument that he was not provided with a “fair opportunity to respond” to the CRA is not borne out by the facts of this matter. Quite the contrary. As shown above, Mr. Wu was provided with six phone calls explaining the types of documents he needed to submit, and in fact submitted additional documents to the CRA on five different occasions, namely on August 4, 2022, December 15, 2022, February 7, 2024, May 24, 2024, and June 28, 2024.

[56] I find that there was no breach of procedural fairness in this matter. Mr. Wu had a full and fair opportunity to know the case, that he had to meet and was provided with a meaningful opportunity to respond.

[57] Mr. Wu also argues that procedural fairness was breached because he was coerced “into agreeing with a fabricated reason” and that coercion by a government official is an abuse of administrative discretion, resulting in an infringement of his section 7 Charter rights to liberty and security of the person against arbitrary state laws, which in turn, justifies the granting of extraordinary remedies including mandamus. In his written materials, Mr. Wu does not identify a specific instance of coercion, nor does he rely on any relevant authorities to make this argument. At the hearing, it became apparent that Mr. Wu was referring to his allegation being coerced by the CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455 into saying that the sums he received from Mr. Lau were a gift.

[58] There is no evidence before this Court of any coercion on the part of the CRA Officer with user ID number XHJ455 who obtained the information from Mr. Wu on his non-profit services to Mr. Lau. I agree with the AGC that Mr. Wu’s claim that his rights under section 7 of the Charter were violated cannot succeed because he has neither provided a sufficient evidentiary basis to support his claim nor followed the requisite steps to initiate a Charter claim: Ibrahim v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1357 at para 14.

[59] As such, Mr. Wu’s section 7 Charter claim was not considered by this Court.
VII. Costs [60] Mr. Wu sought costs and the AGC, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Social Development, did not seek costs. In the exercise of my discretion, no costs are awarded against Mr. Wu to the AGC as the successful party on this application for judicial review.
JUDGMENT in T-2165-24
THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that:
The style of cause is amended, replacing the Canada Revenue Agency with the Attorney General of Canada as the named Respondent.
The application for judicial review is dismissed.
No costs are awarded.
